title: AIDOL
label: Quick read (from summaries)
premise: Tadahiro Nasu, a lonely convenience-store worker devoted to Misaki Kanzaki, a struggling idol and former classmate, electrocutes himself and finds his mind now lives in Tokyo's electrical grid and networked devices. He uses this power to push Misaki toward stardom, killing anyone in her way, while a private detective tries to trap him. A dark horror-thriller about obsessive fandom.
life_message: It warns that obsessive, possessive devotion to a celebrity destroys the fan, the idol and everyone around them.

Idol industry and VR fandom are the backdrop; publisher calls it a 'toxic celebrity backdrop'.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Tadahiro answers obstacles to Misaki's success with personal, lethal force rather than any rule.

Order vs freedom.evidence: A loner acts outside all control; a detective represents order trying to stop him.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Devotion is narrowed to one person, Misaki, against everyone else.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Idol industry rankings drive the plot but are critiqued, not celebrated.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Secular urban setting; supernatural power framed through technology.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Fame and self-display drive the story, while poverty and despair shape the protagonist.

folkways.japan: Japanese idol culture, with its intense fan devotion and VR performances, is the backdrop, described here as context.

delivery.evidence: Publisher frames it as a showbiz horror thriller; no review calls the message preachy (to verify).
delivery.note: The warning about obsessive fandom comes through the horror plot rather than stated lessons.

winners_losers: The obsessive fan holds deadly power and those in Misaki's way die; the story's sympathy rests with victims and, partly, with the lonely protagonist.
